title_en: Wang Yuguo v. China Life Insurance Company, Huai'an City Chuzhou Sub-branch — insurance contract dispute
ruling_gist_en: An insurance company's use of standard terms in an insurance contract to limit the treatment method for the insured upon illness is neither consistent with medical practice nor with the purpose of entering into the insurance contract. The insured has the right to choose the best treatment method according to his or her own condition, and need not be bound by the treatment method restrictions in the insurance contract. The insurance company cannot relieve itself of insurance liability on the ground that the insured did not choose the treatment method specified in the insurance contract.

full_text_en:
Wang Yuguo v. China Life Insurance Company Limited, Huai'an Chuzhou Sub-branch — Dispute over Insurance Contract

Ruling Summary

Where an insurance company restricts the treatment method for an insured person's illness through a standard clause in the insurance contract, such restriction is inconsistent with medical practice and defeats the purpose of concluding the insurance contract. The insured person has the right to choose the optimal treatment method based on his or her own condition and is not bound by the treatment method specified in the insurance contract. The insurance company cannot be exempted from its insurance liability on the ground that the insured person did not choose the treatment method designated in the insurance contract.

Plaintiff: Wang Yuguo, male, 52 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Huai'an, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: China Life Insurance Company Limited, Huai'an Chuzhou Sub-branch, domiciled at Zhenhuai Lou East Road, Huai'an District, Huai'an City, Jiangsu Province.

Responsible Person: Li Xuebiao, Manager of the Company.

The plaintiff, Wang Yuguo, filed a lawsuit with the Huai'an District People's Court of Huai'an, Jiangsu Province, against the defendant, China Life Insurance Company Limited, Huai'an Chuzhou Sub-branch (hereinafter referred to as "Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch"), regarding a dispute over an insurance contract.

Plaintiff's Allegations

On July 30, 2009, the plaintiff and the defendant entered into a Kangning Lifetime Insurance Contract. Article 5, Paragraph 1 of the contract stipulates: If, 180 days after the effective date of the contract, the insured person first suffers from a major disease as defined in this contract, Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch shall pay major disease insurance at twice the basic sum insured. The insured sum of the contract is RMB 20,000. On February 12, 2011, the plaintiff was diagnosed with aortic dissection at Huai'an First People's Hospital and was advised to transfer to a higher-level hospital for continued treatment. On February 22, 2011, the plaintiff underwent surgical treatment at Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital, incurring medical expenses of over RMB 100,000. The plaintiff repeatedly requested the defendant to settle the claim, but the defendant refused to pay the insurance benefits. The plaintiff requests the court to order the defendant to pay the plaintiff insurance benefits of RMB 40,000 and to bear the litigation costs and appraisal fees.

Defendant's Defense

The defendant argues that it is true that the plaintiff, Wang Yuguo, entered into a Kangning Lifetime Insurance Contract (2007 Edition) with the defendant on July 30, 2009. However, because the disease (surgery) suffered by the plaintiff does not fall within the scope of insurance liability stipulated in the contract, the defendant requests the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

Facts Found by the Court of First Instance

On July 30, 2009, the plaintiff and the defendant entered into an insurance contract. The contract provided: The insurance type is Kangning Lifetime Insurance Contract (2007 Revised Edition), with a premium amount of RMB 20,000, and a lifetime insurance period. Article 5, Paragraph 1 of the Kangning Lifetime Insurance Clause (2007 Revised Edition) stipulates: If, 180 days after the effective date of the contract, the insured person first suffers from a major disease as defined in this contract, the Company shall pay major disease insurance at twice the basic sum insured. Article 23, "Names and Definitions of Major Diseases," provides as follows: "10. Aortic surgery means, for the treatment of aortic disease, the actual performance of resection, replacement, or repair of diseased aortic vessels through thoracotomy or laparotomy. The aorta refers to the thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta, excluding the branch vessels of the thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta. Endovascular procedures are not covered by the insurance." After the contract was signed, the plaintiff paid premiums totaling RMB 4,600 on August 1, 2009, and August 10, 2010. On February 12, 2011, the plaintiff was diagnosed with aortic dissection (Stanford Type B) at Huai'an First People's Hospital and was advised to transfer to a higher-level hospital for continued treatment. From February 17, 2011, to March 4, 2011, the plaintiff underwent covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection at Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital. The plaintiff requested the defendant to pay the insurance benefits but was unsuccessful; thus, he filed this lawsuit.

On April 27, 2012, upon the application of the plaintiff, Wang Yuguo, the court commissioned the Forensic Identification Institute of Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital to conduct an appraisal on the following matters: "(1) Whether the aortic dissection (Stanford Type B) suffered by Wang Yuguo is an aortic disease; (2) Whether the covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection has less trauma, lower surgical mortality, and lower complication rates than the thoracotomy surgery stipulated in Article 23, Item 10 of the China Life Insurance Company Limited Kangning Lifetime Insurance Clause (2007 Revised Edition); (3) Whether the covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection constitutes aortic surgery as stipulated in Article 23, Item 10 of the China Life Insurance Company Limited Kangning Lifetime Insurance Clause (2007 Revised Edition); (4) Whether the patient's condition is more suitable for covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection and whether it falls within the scope of aortic repair." The Institute issued Forensic Clinical Identification Report No. 087 [2012] on June 11, 2012, with the following expert opinion: "The aortic dissection (Stanford Type B) suffered by Wang Yuguo is an aortic disease; the covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection has less trauma, lower surgical mortality, and lower complication rates than the thoracotomy surgery stipulated in Article 23, Item 10 of the China Life Insurance Company Limited Kangning Lifetime Insurance Clause (2007 Revised Edition); the covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection is aortic surgery, but it does not require thoracotomy; the patient's condition is more suitable for covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection, which falls within the scope of interventional aortic repair." On July 10, 2012, the Institute issued a response: "1. With the advancement of medical technology, surgical procedures have been developing towards minimally invasive approaches. Many surgeries that previously required thoracotomy or laparotomy have been replaced by endoscopic or interventional procedures. The disease suffered by the subject, Wang Yuguo, is aortic dissection (Stanford Type B), and this condition is more suitable for interventional covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection. The covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection performed on him is aortic surgery and falls within the scope of interventional aortic repair. Compared with traditional thoracotomy, it has the advantages of less trauma, lower mortality, and lower complication rates, and it has already replaced traditional thoracotomy. 2. With reference to Article 23, Item 10 of the China Life Insurance Company Limited Kangning Lifetime Insurance Clause (2007 Revised Edition) provided by the commissioning party, which states that 'aortic surgery means, for the treatment of aortic disease, the actual performance of resection, replacement, or repair of diseased aortic vessels through thoracotomy or laparotomy...', the covered stent graft exclusion for aortic dissection received by the subject is aortic surgery. Although the approach differs from thoracotomy, the purpose is the same. Because it does not require thoracotomy, the trauma is less. Based on our knowledge of forensic medicine and clinical medicine, the original intent of aortic surgery is to treat aortic disease. It is reasonable to adopt a treatment method with less trauma, lower mortality, and lower complication rates. The replacement of old surgical approaches with new ones represents scientific progress; the specific surgical approach is not the core element of this clause. 3. The opinions expressed in our institute's appraisal are clear. The focus of the conflict in this case arises from the fact that the insurance clause lags behind current medical technology." The plaintiff paid appraisal fees of RMB 5,380 (examination fee of RMB 5,280 and outpatient fee of RMB 100).

Opinion of the Court of First Instance

The Kangning Lifetime Insurance Contract entered into by the plaintiff and the defendant represents the true intention of both parties and does not violate any mandatory provisions of laws or administrative regulations. Therefore, it should be deemed legal and valid, binding on both parties, who must strictly exercise their rights and perform their obligations in accordance with the contract. In this case, the plaintiff and the defendant have no dispute over the existence of the insurance relationship between them or the fact that the plaintiff suffers from an aortic disease. The only dispute is whether the plaintiff's treatment of aortic dissection using covered stent graft exclusion without thoracotomy falls within the scope of insurance liability. The insurance contract clearly stipulates that the scope of insurance for major diseases includes "aortic surgery." Article 23, Item 10 of the contract is an explanation and description of the medical term "aortic surgery" to further define the scope of insurance liability. "Aortic surgery" means surgery for the treatment of aortic disease, and the aorta refers to the thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta, excluding branch vessels. Therefore, diseases of the thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta should fall within the insurance liability scope for major diseases under the Kangning Lifetime Insurance Contract entered into by the plaintiff and the defendant. In this case, according to the forensic identification report and response from the Forensic Identification Institute of Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital, the aortic dissection (Stanford Type B) suffered by the plaintiff, Wang Yuguo, is an aortic disease and falls within the insurance liability scope for major diseases under the Kangning Lifetime Insurance Contract. The provision in Article 23, Item 10 of the contract regarding "the actual performance of resection, replacement, or repair of diseased aortic vessels through thoracotomy or laparotomy" is clearly not an explanation or description of disease symptoms but rather a restriction on the treatment method for the disease, which precludes the insured person's right to choose the treatment method. According to common understanding, a major disease is not necessarily linked to a specific treatment method. When suffering from a major disease, the insured person will often consider his or her own physical condition and choose a treatment method with less trauma, lower mortality, and lower complication rates to effectively treat the disease, without thinking that he or she must ensure the payment of major disease insurance benefits by adopting the treatment method limited by the insurer. The insurer's act of limiting the insured person's right to claim benefits by restricting the treatment method, thereby exempting itself from insurance liability, should be deemed invalid under Article 19 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China. Moreover, with the advancement of medical technology, surgical procedures have been developing towards minimally invasive approaches, and many surgeries that previously required thoracotomy or laparotomy have been replaced by endoscopic or interventional procedures. Since the insurance period for major diseases is often very long, even lifelong, it is inconsistent with the laws of medical development for an insurer to limit the treatment method for a major disease based on the treatment method at the time of insurance. An insurance company cannot refuse to settle a claim simply because the insured person did not choose the treatment method specified in the contract.

Accordingly, the Huai'an District People's Court of Huai'an, Jiangsu Province, pursuant to Article 107 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 23 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 128 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and after deliberation by the Judicial Committee of the court, rendered the following judgment on September 6, 2012:

The defendant, China Life Insurance Company Limited, Huai'an Chuzhou Sub-branch, shall pay the plaintiff, Wang Yuguo, insurance benefits of RMB 40,000 within ten days after the effective date of this judgment.

Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch appealed the judgment of first instance to the Huai'an Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province, arguing: (1) The Court of First Instance erred in fact-finding; the disease suffered by the appellee, Wang Yuguo, does not fall within the payment scenario for aortic disease stipulated in the insurance contract between the parties. The scenario for payment of insurance benefits stipulated in the contract is: aortic disease for which an actual thoracotomy or laparotomy has been performed. (2) The forensic identification opinion of Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital should not be adopted; the appellee's disease was treated at Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital, which has a conflict of interest with the appellee. The appellant requests the Court of Second Instance to ascertain the facts and, by amended judgment, dismiss Wang Yuguo's claims.

The appellee, Wang Yuguo, argued in response: The Court of First Instance found the facts clearly, applied the law correctly, and followed proper procedures. The appellee requests the Court of Second Instance to dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

The Huai'an Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province confirmed the facts found by the Court of First Instance after the second-instance trial.

The issues in dispute at the second instance were: (1) Whether the appellant, Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch, should pay the appellee, Wang Yuguo, insurance benefits of RMB 40,000; (2) Whether the forensic identification conclusion of Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital can be used as a basis for deciding this case.

Opinion of the Court of Second Instance

First, on July 30, 2009, the insurance contract entered into by the appellant, Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch, and the appellee, Wang Yuguo, represented their true intention and did not violate any prohibitive provisions of laws or administrative regulations; it was legal and valid. Both parties should perform their respective obligations in accordance with the insurance contract. Regarding the first issue in dispute, because Article 23 of the Kangning Lifetime Insurance Clause (2007 Revised Edition) of the contract entered into by the parties is a provision by which the appellant, Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch, restricts the appellee, Wang Yuguo's right to obtain claims payments by limiting the treatment method, thereby exempting itself from insurance liability, such clause is invalid under Article 19 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China. Moreover, Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch has no dispute that the disease suffered by Wang Yuguo is an aortic disease. The appellant's argument that the disease suffered by Wang Yuguo does not fall within the scenario for payment of insurance benefits under the insurance contract cannot be sustained and is not accepted by this court. (2) The appellant, Life Insurance Chuzhou Sub-branch, argues that Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital, as a treatment institution, cannot serve as a forensic identification institution. This argument has no legal basis, and both parties acknowledged that the identification institution was jointly chosen by the parties.

In summary, the appellant's grounds of appeal cannot be sustained and are not accepted by this court. The Court of First Instance found the facts clearly and rendered a correct judgment; therefore, the judgment should be affirmed.

Accordingly, the Huai'an Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province, pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on November 13, 2012:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
